exam: What bedside signs would you look for to suspect a Zenker diverticulum? — Look for regurgitation of undigested food, neck gurgle on swallowing, and halitosis; these point to a pharyngeal pouch.
A patient with dysphagia and weight loss has a normal chest X‑ray. What is your next step? — Order a barium swallow to visualise a possible cervical diverticulum.
How does impaired cricopharyngeal relaxation lead to a diverticulum? — Failure to open the upper oesophageal sphincter raises intraluminal pressure, forcing the mucosa through Killian’s dehiscence.

What are the key differences between Zenker diverticulum and a laryngocele? — Zenker is a posterior pharyngeal pouch that fills with food; laryngocele is an anterior air‑filled sac that enlarges with Valsalva.
When is surgical intervention indicated? — When the diverticulum is medium/large, causes aspiration, recurrent pneumonia, or significant weight loss.

Why is a stapled endoscopic diverticulotomy preferred over open surgery when available? — It is less invasive, has shorter hospital stay, and lower morbidity while achieving myotomy and pouch closure.

What antibiotic regimen would you choose for aspiration pneumonia in this patient and why? — Amoxicillin‑clavulanate covers typical oral flora; avoid macrolides if QT prolongation risk or drug interactions.

How would you manage a perforated Zenker diverticulum in a setting without thoracic surgery? — Stabilise with nil per os, broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics, and arrange urgent transfer to a centre with surgical capability.
ai.title: Zenker Diverticulum
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Zenker diverticulum is a pulsion diverticulum of the hypopharynx that causes dysphagia, regurgitation and aspiration. Diagnosis relies on bedside clues and imaging, and treatment ranges from dietary measures to endoscopic or surgical repair.

b: Pulsion (false) diverticulum, not a true wall‑layer diverticulum
Located posteriorly at the cervical oesophagus
sections.p: A Zenker diverticulum is an outpouching through Killian's dehiscence, a weak area between the cricopharyngeus and inferior constrictor muscles. It forms when the upper oesophageal sphincter fails to relax, creating high intraluminal pressure.

t.b: Confirms presence, size and neck of diverticulum; shows a classic ‘bird's beak’ or ‘pouch’ posterior to the oesophagus
Visualises the diverticulum orifice and rules out malignancy; if unavailable, rely on careful oropharyngeal exam
May show an air‑filled mediastinal mass; useful when barium study not possible

b: Small: occasional dysphagia, no aspiration
Medium: frequent regurgitation, mild aspiration
Large: chronic aspiration, weight loss, possible airway compromise
sections.p: Severity is graded by size and symptom burden; no universal numeric stage, but clinicians use small (<2 cm), medium (2–4 cm) and large (>4 cm) categories.

b: Neuromuscular disorders (e.g., Parkinson’s, post‑stroke)
Chronic alcohol use causing cricopharyngeal spasm
Upper‑airway infections (TB, HIV‑related neuropathy) that affect swallowing coordination
sections.p: The primary cause is impaired relaxation of the cricopharyngeal muscle, often idiopathic. Secondary contributors common in low‑resource settings include:

b: Regurgitated food may be seen in the oral cavity or on the neck dressing
Weight loss and dehydration in advanced cases
A palpable neck mass that gurgles on swallowing (Boyce’s sign)
sections.p: Patients typically report progressive dysphagia for solids then liquids, nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food, cough after meals, and occasional halitosis.
Imaging confirms the diagnosis; endoscopy evaluates mucosal health; basic labs assess nutritional status.

t.b: Shows diverticulum size and neck; if unavailable, use water‑soluble contrast or bedside swallow test
Detects ulceration or carcinoma within the pouch; if not possible, refer for surgical assessment
Identify anemia or electrolyte loss from chronic vomiting

b: Aspiration pneumonia
Diverticulum perforation leading to mediastinitis
Bleeding from ulcerated mucosa
Weight loss causing malnutrition
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent attention.

b: Dietary modification: soft diet, upright position after meals
Speech‑language therapy to improve swallowing coordination
Endoscopic stapled diverticulotomy (preferred where equipment exists)
Open diverticulectomy with cricopharyngeal myotomy if endoscopy unavailable
Antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) – avoid macrolides if QT prolongation risk
sections.p: Initial care focuses on symptom control and aspiration prevention; definitive therapy is endoscopic or open surgical repair.

b: Repeat barium swallow at 6 months if symptoms persist
Continued swallowing exercises
Avoid large boluses and rapid eating
Treat underlying neuromuscular disease
sections.p: After repair, monitor for recurrence, dysphagia and aspiration. Long‑term measures reduce risk of new diverticula.

b: Pharyngeal pouch secondary to malignancy
Laryngocele (air‑filled sac of the laryngeal ventricle)
Cervical oesophageal web
sections.p: Several cervical oesophageal conditions mimic Zenker diverticulum.

b: Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude a small diverticulum
Absence of cough does not rule out silent aspiration
sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe chest pain after vomiting (possible perforation)
High‑grade fever with productive cough (aspiration pneumonia)
Rapid weight loss or inability to swallow liquids
